intro: The simplest way to read and write a device over Ethernet. A device keeps its data in registers: numbered boxes of 16 bits, each holding one whole number from 0 to 65535. A client, the device that asks, requests some registers by number and gets their contents back. Nothing in the protocol says what a register means: that is in the device's manual.
plain: Modbus TCP lets one machine read and change the numbers inside another machine over a computer network. Picture a wall of numbered lockers inside the device, each holding one number. A computer asks "what is in locker 100?", and the device answers with what is inside. Only the device's manual says what each locker means, such as the power right now or a limit.

connect.title: Open a connection
connect.text: The plant controller, the computer that runs the solar plant, connects to the inverter, the box that turns solar power into grid power. It opens a TCP connection (a reliable link over the network) on port 502, the port kept for Modbus. Modbus TCP has no login and no start command: the connection is enough.

read.title: Read the power
read.text: The manual lists active power (the power the inverter delivers right now) at register 40101. The first digit, 4, only names the kind of register. The rest, 0101, counts from 1, but the wire counts from 0, so the controller asks for address 100. The answer is 4 bytes: one 32-bit float (a number with a decimal point) that fills two registers. Its value: 4820.5 kW.

limit.title: Set a power limit
limit.text: The grid operator, the company that runs the power lines, asks for less power. The controller writes 3000 into address 200, the power limit in kW. The inverter answers with an exact copy of the request. That copy means: done.

check.title: Check it worked
check.text: Modbus never reports a change by itself. The client must ask again, and again: this is called polling. Six seconds later the power is 2998.7 kW.

mistake.title: A wrong address
mistake.text: A new script sends the manual's number, 40101, as it is, instead of address 100. The inverter has no register there. So it answers with an exception, an error message, instead of data.

frames.tcp: Open a TCP connection to port 502
frames.write-req: Set the power limit to 3000 kW

notes.tcp: Plain TCP: three short messages that open the connection. No Modbus bytes yet. Many devices accept only a few connections at a time, so a client keeps its connection open and reuses it.

tid-1.name: Transaction ID 1
tid-1.note: A number the client picks. The answer carries the same one, so the client can match each answer to its request.

tid-2.name: Transaction ID 2
tid-2.note: The next request, the next number.

tid-3.name: Transaction ID 3
tid-3.note: Request 3 and its answer both carry 3.

tid-4.name: Transaction ID 4
tid-4.note: Even an error answer carries the request's number.

len-6.name: Length
len-6.note: 6 bytes follow: the unit ID and 5 more bytes.

unit.name: Unit ID 1
unit.note: Picks one device behind a gateway, a box that links several devices to one network address. This inverter answers to 1.

fc03.name: Function 03
fc03.note: 0x03: read holding registers, the registers a client may read and write.

fc06-echo.name: Function 06
fc06-echo.note: The answer to a write repeats the request byte for byte.

fc83.name: Function 83
fc83.note: 0x83 = 0x03 + 0x80. The function code with its highest bit set means: this is an error answer.

addr-40101.name: Address 40101
addr-40101.note: 0x9CA5 = 40101: the manual's number, sent as it is. Wrong: the inverter has nothing there.

reg-100.name: Register 100
reg-100.note: 0xA400: the low half of the float. This inverter sends the low 16-bit half first, a word order called CDAB.

reg-101.name: Register 101
reg-101.note: 0x4596: the high half. Put back in order, high then low, 0x4596A400 is 4820.5 (kW).

code-02.name: Exception 02
code-02.note: Illegal data address: the register does not exist. 01 would mean an unknown function, 03 a bad value.

a-table.name: Table
a-table.note: 4: a holding register, read with function 03. 3 is an input register (read only, function 04), 1 a discrete input (a read-only on/off bit), 0 a coil (an on/off bit a client can write).

a-number.name: Number
a-number.note: 0101: the 101st register. Manuals count from 1, the wire counts from 0.

facts.standard: Modbus Application Protocol V1.1b3 and Modbus Messaging on TCP/IP V1.0b (Modbus Organization)
facts.between: Client (plant controller, SCADA, logger) → server (inverter, meter, battery)
facts.security: None. Anyone who reaches port 502 can read and write. Modbus/TCP Security adds TLS encryption on port 802.
facts.frames: A 7-byte MBAP header (transaction ID, protocol ID, length, unit ID), then a function code and its data
facts.since: 1979 on serial lines (Modicon), on TCP since 1999

tips: Find out whether the manual counts registers from 0 or from 1. One register off reads half of one value and half of the next, and that can look almost right.
Check the word order of 32-bit values, which 16-bit half comes first, against a value you know, such as the power on the inverter's display. Many devices send the low word first (CDAB).
Many devices accept only a few TCP connections. A test tool left connected can lock out the plant controller.
Modbus has no passwords. Keep port 502 inside the plant network, and never let it be reached from the internet.

anatomy.register: A register number from a manual, and the address that goes on the wire

playground.encoder: This inverter sends a 32-bit float low word first (CDAB). Type a value to see its bytes, and what the same bytes mean when read in another order.
playground.file: The inverter's register map, from its manual: what each register holds. The controller must be set up with the same addresses, types and word order.
playground.unit: The unit ID the inverter answers to.
playground.offset: How to turn a register number into an address. Look for this in every manual: some count from 0.
playground.float: Two registers, one float, low word first. The controller must be set to CDAB.
playground.scaled: A whole number with a scale: divide by 100, so 5001 means 50.01 Hz.
playground.uint32: Also two registers, also low word first: a whole number too big for one register.
playground.limit: Writable: the limit the controller sets in step 3.
playground.fallback: If the controller stops writing for this long, the inverter goes back to its fallback setting. A lost link then does not leave the plant stuck at an old limit.
